Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verses 1–4:

(p-136) Surat adh-Dhariyat

﴿By the winds that scatter dust⁠—﴾ that is, the winds that scatter the dust and other things. It has also been read with the ta' assimilated into the dhal (idgham).

﴿And those that carry a heavy load⁠—﴾ that is, the clouds that carry rain, or the winds that carry the clouds. It has also been read as "wiqran" (with fath), treating the carried load by the verbal noun (tasmiyat al-mahmul bil-masdar), i.e., naming the thing carried by its verbal noun.

﴿And those that glide along with ease⁠—﴾ that is, the ships that sail on the sea, or the winds blowing in their directions, or the clouds moving through the air by the driving of the winds, or the stars running in their orbits and mansions. "Yusran" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a running that is easy (jaryan dha yusrin).

﴿And those that distribute the command⁠—﴾ that is, the angels who distribute affairs, such as rains, provisions and other things; or the clouds through which God Most High distributes the provision of His servants. It has also been permitted that all of these be taken to mean the winds, treating the difference of description as if it were a difference of essence, for just as they scatter what they scatter, they stir up the clouds, carry them, move through the air with easy motion, and distribute the rains by turning the clouds across the regions. If the things sworn by are taken as different essences, then the fa' (in "fa-") indicates the sequence of the oaths according to the differing degrees of their indication of perfect power; otherwise, it indicates the sequence of the actions that proceed from the wind, for it scatters the vapors into the air until they coalesce into clouds, then runs with them, spreading them out toward what they were commanded, and thus distributes the rain.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verses 5–6:

Allah's saying: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is true﴾, ﴿and indeed the judgment (al-din) is surely to occur﴾ is the answer to the oath (al-qasam). In singling out the things mentioned for the oath by them, there is an indication (ramz) of their testifying to the realization of the content of the sentence sworn to, insofar as they are wondrous matters contrary to what nature requires; so whoever has power over them is capable of the promised resurrection (al-ba'th). The "ma" (in ﴿ma tu'adun﴾) is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah). The description of the promise as "true" is like the description of a life as "pleasing" (in ﴿fi 'ishatin radiyah﴾). Al-din means the recompense (al-jaza'), and its "occurrence" (wuquʻuhu) means its coming to pass (husuluhu).(p-137)

The description of the promise as "true" is like the description of a life as "pleasing" (in ﴿fi 'ishatin radiyah﴾). Al-din means the recompense (al-jaza'), and its "occurrence" (wuquʻuhu) means its coming to pass (husuluhu).(p-137)

﴿By the sky, the one possessing ḥubuk﴾. Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatādah, and ʿIkrimah said: "It means the sky of even, well-made creation." Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: "It means the sky of adornment." Mujāhid said: "It means the one whose structure is firmly made." Muqātil, al-Kalbī, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: "It means the one with paths." The meaning is either the sensible paths, which are the courses of the stars, or the intellectual paths that the reflecting scholars (al-nuzzār) travel, or the stars themselves, since they have paths. It is narrated from al-Ḥasan that ḥubkuhā means its stars, where they adorn it, as the figured fabric (al-muwashsha) is adorned with the lines of its weaving. The word is either the plural of ḥibāk or ḥabīkah, like mithāl and mithal, or ṭarīqah and ṭuruq. It has also been read as "al-ḥibk" on the pattern of "al-silk," "al-ḥabak" like "al-jabal," "al-ḥabk" like "al-barq," "al-ḥibak" like "al-niʿam," and "al-ḥibik" like "al-ibil."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 8:

﴿Indeed, you are in a discordant saying.﴾ That is: contradictory, self-conflicting. This is their saying concerning him, upon him be prayer and peace: at one time he is a poet (shā'ir), at another a sorcerer (sāḥir), and at another a madman (majnūn). And concerning the Noble Qur'an: at one time it is poetry (shi'r), at another sorcery (siḥr), and at another fables (asāṭīr). In this reply there is support for the view that ḥubuk (the "weaving" or "fine structure" of the sky, in the preceding oath) means "evenness" (istiwā', harmony and consistency), as is hinted at by what is transmitted from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, that the saying of the disbelievers is not even (mustawī) but is rather contradictory and discordant. It has also been said: the point of this oath is to liken their sayings, in their divergence and the conflict of their aims, to the paths of the heavens in their remoteness and the difference of their destinations. But this is not the right view.

Translation:

﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away.﴾ That is: whoever is diverted from the Qur'an or from the Messenger, may blessings and peace be upon him, is turned away, for there is no diversion more grievous or severe than this. It has also been said: whoever is turned away from it is one who was turned away in the knowledge and decree of God Most High. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the "divergent speech," in the sense that the falsehood of whoever is turned away proceeds from that speech. It has been read as "man afaka" ("whoever has deceived") concerning that speech, and it has been read as "man afaka" meaning: whoever deceived people, namely the Quraysh, since they used to bar people from faith.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 10:

﴿Cursed be the conjecturers﴾ This is a supplication against them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Cursed be man, how ungrateful he is!﴾ Its origin is the supplication for killing and destruction, then it came to function like "la'ana" (cursed). "Al-kharrasun" (the conjecturers): the liars who estimate what has no validity, and they are the people of the divergent speech. It is as if it were said: "Cursed be these conjecturers." It was also read "qatala al-kharrasina," meaning: may Allah kill them.

Translation:

﴿Those who are in heedlessness﴾ (ghamrah), that is, in ignorance and misguidance.

﴿Are heedless﴾ (sahun), that is, unmindful of what they have been commanded.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 12:

﴿They ask, "When is the Day of Judgment?"﴾ That is: when will the Day of Recompense occur? However, this is not a request for information in the true sense, but rather a request for hastening, mockingly. And it has been recited as "Iyyan" with a kasra on the hamza.

Verse 13: ﴿On the Day they will be tried over the Fire.﴾ It is an answer to the question: that is, it happens on the Day they are burned over the Fire (p-138) and tormented. It is also permissible for "yawma" (the Day) to be the predicate of an omitted subject, that is: it is "the Day they are..." etc. The fatha (vowel) on it is due to its being attached to a particle that is indeclinable (mabni). This is supported by the fact that it was also read with a damma (raf').

Taste your trial. (This is) what you used to seek to hasten.

This is an exposition by Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim). The phrase ﴿ذُوقُوا فِتْنَتَكُمْ﴾ means: with this being said to them as a spoken address. His words, the Exalted, ﴿هَذا الَّذِي كُنْتُمْ بِهِ تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾ form a sentence of subject and predicate (mubtada' wa khabar, the nominal sentence) that falls under the implied verb of speech, meaning: this is what you used to seek to hasten by way of mockery. It is also permissible for ﴿هَذا﴾ to be a substitute (badal) for "fitnatakum," with the interpretation of it as "the punishment," and the relative clause ﴿الَّذِي﴾ being its qualifier (sifah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 15:

﴿Indeed, the God-conscious (al-muttaqun) are in gardens and springs.﴾ Its true nature (kunh) cannot be reached, and its measure cannot be estimated.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 16:

﴿Taking what their Lord has given them.﴾ That is: accepting what He has bestowed upon them, content with it, on the meaning that everything He has given them is good and pleasing, received with good acceptance.

﴿Indeed they were before that⁠﴾ in the world.

﴿doers of good﴾ That is: performing their righteous deeds, bringing them as they ought to be done; therefore they attained what they attained of the great triumph. The meaning of ihsan (excellence, doing good) in summary is what he (ﷺ) alluded to in his saying: "That you worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 17:

It has been explained by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They used to sleep but little of the night﴾. That is: they used to sleep during a small portion of the night, on the basis that "qalilan" (little) is a adverbial of time (zarf); or: they used to sleep a little sleep (hujuaan qalilan), on the basis that it is an attribute of the verbal noun (masdar). The "ma" is superfluous (zā'idah) in both cases. It is also permissible for it to be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah) or a relative pronoun (mawsulah) in the nominative position as the subject (fa'iliyyah) of "qalilan", meaning: they used to be little of the night in their sleeping, or [the portion] in which they slept. In it there is an intensification (lil-mubalaghat) in minimizing their sleep and their rest, through the mention of "little" and "the night", which is the time of rest, and "hujua" (sleeping), which is the brief dozing of sleep, and the addition of "ma". There is no justification for making "ma" a negation, meaning that they do not sleep a little of the night but rather spend all of it in worship, because a negating "ma" does not govern what comes after it over what comes before it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 18:

﴿And in the hours before dawn they would seek forgiveness﴾. That is: despite how little they slept and how much they performed tahajjud (night prayer), they persistently sought forgiveness at the hours before dawn, as if they had spent their night committing sins. And in the construction of the verb upon the pronoun (هم, "they") there is an indication that they are the most deserving of being described as those who seek forgiveness, as if they were the ones specially characterized by it, because of their constancy in it and their prolixity in it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 19:

﴿And in their wealth there was a right﴾ i.e., a generous portion which they would impose upon themselves, seeking nearness to Allah the Exalted and out of compassion for the people.

﴿For the beggar and the deprived﴾ for the one who asks, and for the one who abstains from asking (al-mutaʿaffif), whom people think to be rich, so he is deprived of charity.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 20:

﴿And in the earth are signs for those of certainty﴾ That is: clear proofs of His exalted affairs, in detail, in that it is spread out like a smoothed carpet, and in it are roads and wide passages for those who move about its regions and travel along its sides, and in it are plains and mountains, land and sea, adjoining tracts, gushing springs, and diverse minerals, and [in that] it brings forth plants of various colors, kinds of trees, and varieties of fruits differing in color, taste, and fragrance. And in it are creatures dispersed, all of which have been arranged and ordered for the benefits and welfare of its inhabitants, in their health and in their sickness.

**"And in yourselves [too are signs]."** That is: and in yourselves are signs, for there is nothing in the world except that there is a counterpart to it in the human self, which points by its indication to what it alone possesses of beneficial forms, beautiful appearances, wondrous compositions, the capacity for marvellous acts, the derivation of diverse crafts, and the gathering together of varied perfections.

**"Will you not then see?"** That is: will you not look, so that you see with the eye of insight?

﴿And in the heaven is your provision﴾, that is: the causes of your provision, or its decree (taqdiruh). It has also been said that by "the heaven" is meant the clouds, and by "the provision" is meant the rain, for it is the cause of sustenance (al-aqwat).

﴿And what you are promised﴾ of reward, because Paradise is in the seventh heaven, or because the deeds and their rewards are written and decreed in the heaven. It has also been said that it is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is the statement of the Exalted:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 23:

﴿So by the Lord of the heaven and the earth, indeed it is the truth﴾ — on the basis that the pronoun refers to "what" (ma, i.e., the promise/provision mentioned earlier). As for on the first reading, it refers either to Him or to what was mentioned of the signs and the provision, on the basis that it is used metaphorically for the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah).

﴿Like your speech﴾ — i.e., just as there is no doubt for you that you speak, so you should not doubt its truth. Its being in the accusative is either as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the pronoun hidden in "haqq" (truth), or as a description of an omitted verbal noun (masdar), meaning: indeed it is true with the truth of your speech. It has been said that it is built on the fathah (vowel), because it is annexed to something indeclinable, namely "ma" when it is a reference to a thing, and "anna" with what follows it if "ma" is considered superfluous (za'ida); its position is in the nominative, as a description of "haqq." The recitation with the nominative supports this.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 24:

﴿Has there reached you the story of the honored guests of Abraham?﴾ This is an exaltation of the importance of the story and an alert that it is not among the things the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) knew by any means other than revelation. The word "ḍayf" (guest) is originally a verbal noun (maṣdar) of "ḍāfahu" (he hosted him), and for this reason it is applied to the singular and the plural alike, like "zawr" (visitors) and "ṣawm" (fasting). They were twelve angels. It is also said: nine, the tenth of whom was Jibril (Gabriel). It is also said: three, namely Jibril, Mika'il (Michael), and another angel with them, peace be upon them all. They were called "guests" either because they were in the form of guests when Abraham (peace be upon him) hosted them, or because they were regarded as guests in his estimation.

﴿The honored﴾ means: honored with Allah the Exalted, or honored in the sight of Abraham, since he served them himself and along with his wife.

﴿إذْ دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ﴾ is a *zarf* (temporal adverbial complement) modifying either *al-hadith* (the story) or the sense of verbal action in *al-day'if* (the guest), or *al-mukramin* (the honored ones) if it is interpreted as referring to Abraham's honoring of them.

﴿فَقالُوا سَلامًا﴾ means: "We greet you with a greeting."

﴿قالَ﴾ means: Abraham said.

﴿سَلامٌ﴾ means: "Peace be upon you." It was changed to the nominative form as a *mubtada'* (nominal subject) in order to express permanence and continuity, so that his greeting would be better than their greeting (p-140). It is also read in the nominative as two forms, and it is read as *silm*, and it is read in the accusative, and the meaning is one.

﴿قَوْمٌ مُنْكَرُونَ﴾ Abraham found them unfamiliar, either because of the greeting, which is the emblem of Islam, or because they were not among the people he knew, or because their appearance and forms differed from what people were accustomed to. It is likely that he, peace be upon him, said this to himself without making them aware of it, and not that he addressed them with it aloud or asked them to identify themselves, as has been said. Otherwise they would have revealed their condition at that point, and he, peace be upon him, would not have undertaken the preparations for hospitality.

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 51, verse 26:

﴿Then he turned quietly to his family﴾, i.e., he went to them secretly away from his guest, for it is part of the courtesy of the host that he hastens to offer him hospitality (al-qira) and hurries to do so, lest he (the guest) hold back, excuse him, or become one who waits. The fa' in His words, ﴿then he brought a fattened calf﴾, is fa' fasiha (the "eloquent" fa', i.e., one that indicates omitted clauses, fasiha being a grammatical term for a fa' that reveals an implied sentence), which is explicitly indicating sentences that have been omitted, relying confidently on the situation to indicate them and signaling the complete speed of bringing the food, as in His words, "Fa-qulna" ("We said"), "Idrib bi-'asaka al-bahr fa-nfalaq" ("Strike the sea with your staff, and it split"). That is, he slaughtered a calf, roasted it (fa-hanadhahu), and then brought it.

《فَقَرَّبَهُ إلَيْهِمْ》 — "So he brought it near to them": by setting it before them, as is customary.

﴿فَقالَ ألا تَأْكُلُونَ﴾ — "and said, 'Will you not eat?'" — expressing disapproval of their not partaking of the food.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 28:

﴿So he conceived fear of them﴾: he concealed it within himself.

﴿Fear﴾: because he imagined that they had come with evil intent. It was also said: it came into his heart that they were angels who had come with punishment.

﴿They said: Do not fear﴾: it was said that Jibril (peace be upon him) touched the calf with his wing, whereupon it got up, ran off and reached its mother, so he recognized them and felt safe from them.

﴿And they gave him good news﴾: and in Surat al-Saffat the wording is "And We gave him good news," meaning through them (through their agency).

﴿Of a boy﴾: he was Ishaq (peace be upon him).

﴿Knowing﴾: when he reached maturity and became full-grown.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 29:

﴿So his wife came forward﴾, Sarah, when she heard their good tidings, to her house, and she had been in a corner, looking at them.

﴿in a cry﴾, in a shriek of (or with) a sound of sharp cry (ṣarīr), and its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial (ḥāl) or as an object, if "aqbalat" is taken to mean "took" (akhadhat), as one says: "aqbala yashtumunī" (he came at me reviling me).

﴿and she struck her face﴾, that is, she slapped it out of shame, because she found the heat of the blood of menstruation (ḥarārat dam al-ṭamth). It is also said: she struck the tips of her fingers against her forehead, as the one who is amazed does.

﴿and said: "An old, barren woman!"﴾, that is: I am an old, barren woman, so how shall I give birth?!

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 30:

﴿They said: "Thus"﴾ — that is, like that noble statement.

﴿Said your Lord﴾ — and we are only conveying (mu'abbiruun), informing you of it from Him, Exalted is He, not that we are saying it from our own selves.

﴿Indeed He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing﴾ — so His word is true and His action is perfectly firm, without doubt. It is narrated that Jibril, peace be upon him, said to her: "Look at the ceiling of your house," and she looked, and behold, its beams were green and fruit-bearing. This exchange was not with Sarah alone, but also with Ibrahim, peace be upon him, as explained in Surah al-Hijr; and it is mentioned here only relying on what was mentioned there, just as Sarah is not mentioned there, relying on what was mentioned here and in Surah Hud.

﴿He said﴾: that is, Ibrahim (peace be upon him), when he knew that they were angels sent on a matter.

﴿So what is your business, O messengers?﴾: that is, what is your grave matter, for which you have been sent, other than the glad tidings?
They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a people who are criminals." ﴿They said: "Indeed we have been sent to a people of criminals."﴾ They mean the people of Lut.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 33:

﴿That We may send down upon them﴾ i.e., after We overturned their towns and made their upper part their lower part, as has been detailed in the other noble surahs.

﴿stones of clay﴾ i.e., clay that has turned to stone, which is the sijjil.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 34:

﴿مُسَوَّمَةً﴾ (musawwamah): sent forth, from asamtu al-ma<u>sh</u>iyah, meaning I let the livestock loose to pasture; or marked, from al-sawmah (al-sumah), which is a mark or sign. Its detailed explanation has already passed in the commentary on Surah Hud.

﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّكَ لِلْمُسْرِفِينَ﴾ "with your Lord, for the transgressors," meaning those who exceed the limit in wickedness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 35:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So We brought out﴾ ... etc. is a narration from Him, Exalted is He, of what befell the people of Lut, peace be upon him, in summary form, after the narration of the words that passed between the angels and Ibrahim, peace be upon him. The fa' (fa) here is fasihah (eloquent, i.e., one that reveals an implied meaning), disclosing sentences that have been omitted, relying on their mention in other places, as if it were said: they carried out what they had been commanded, so We brought out [those who were in it] by Our saying: "So set out with your family" ... etc.

﴿of the believers who were in it﴾ i.e., in the towns of the people of Lut. Its referent is left unmentioned because it was well known.

﴿from among the believers﴾ those who had believed in Lut.

﴿So We found therein no house⁠﴾, that is: no household (ahl bayt) ⁠—

﴿of those who submit (min al-muslimin)⁠﴾. It is said: they were the people of Lut and his two daughters. And it is said: Lut and the household of his that were saved numbered thirteen.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 37:

﴿And We left therein﴾ i.e., in the town.

﴿a sign﴾ i.e., a clear mark indicating what punishment befell them. It has been said: it is those stones, or a layered stone (sakhr mandud) therein, or foul water.

﴿for those who fear the painful punishment﴾ i.e., it is fitting for them to fear it, owing to the soundness of their natural disposition and the tenderness of their hearts, unlike others who have hardened hearts; for they do not regard it or consider it a sign.

And in Musa (Moses) [is a sign], coordinated with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in the earth﴾, or coordinated with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We left therein a sign﴾, in the sense of: "And We made in Musa a sign," like the saying of one who said: "I fed her straw and cold water."

﴿When We sent him﴾: it has been said that it is in the accusative governed by "a sign" (ayah). It has also been said that it is governed by an implied verb, i.e., "existing at the time of Our sending him." It has also been said that it is governed by "We left" (taraknا).

﴿to Fir'awn (Pharaoh) with a manifest authority﴾: this is what appeared at his hands of the dazzling miracles.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 39:**

﴿فَتَوَلّى بِرُكْنِهِ﴾ ﴿So he turned away with his might﴾. That is, he turned away from belief in him and recoiled, like His saying, exalted is He: "And he turned aside with his side" (p-142). It was also said: "He turned away with what he relied upon of his kingdom and his armies," for *al-rukn* (the support, or that on which a thing leans for strength) is a name for that to which a thing leans. It was also read as "*birukunihi*" (بِرُكُنِهِ) with a *damma* on the *kaf*.

﴿وَقالَ ساحِرٌ﴾ ﴿And he said: "A sorcerer"﴾. That is, "He is a sorcerer."

﴿أوْ مَجْنُونٌ﴾ ﴿"Or a madman"﴾. It seems that he attributed the astonishing miraculous feats that appeared at the hands of Moses, upon him be peace, to the jinn, and he was uncertain whether they occurred by his own choice and effort or by other means.

﴿So We seized him and his soldiers, and threw them into the sea.﴾ In this is a clear indication of the greatness of the Lord's power and the utter abasement of Pharaoh and his people.

﴿And he was blameworthy.﴾ That is, he came with what deserved blame, namely disbelief and tyranny. The clause is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial clause) relating to the pronoun in "فَأخَذْناهُ" (*fa-akhadhnāhu*, "so We seized him").

And in ʿAd, when We sent upon them the barren wind (ﷺ)... 

Wait, I must translate exactly. Here is the translation:

And in ʿAd, when We sent upon them the barren wind ﴿الرِّيحَ العَقِيمَ﴾. It was described as "barren" (ʿaqīm) because it destroyed them and cut off their last remnant, or because it carried nothing of good whatsoever, neither bringing rain into being nor fertilizing trees. It is the nakbāʾ (a wind blowing between two cardinal directions), or the dabūr (the west wind), or the janūb (the south wind).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 42:

﴿It leaves nothing that it passes over﴾ i.e., that it has passed over.

﴿But makes it like the crumbled (rameem)﴾ It is everything that has decayed, rotted away and crumbled into pieces, whether of bone, plant matter, or anything else.

And in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a while." That is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Enjoy yourselves in your homes for three days.﴾ It is said: Salih, peace be upon him, said to them, "Tomorrow your faces will become yellow, and the day after tomorrow they will become red, and on the third day they will become black; then the punishment will meet you at dawn."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 44:

﴿So they acted arrogantly towards the command of their Lord﴾, that is, they were arrogant and refused to comply with it.

﴿So the thunderbolt seized them﴾. It is said that when they saw the signs that Salih, peace be upon him, had made clear, namely the yellowing, reddening and blackening of their faces, they resolved to kill him, peace be upon him. But Allah the Exalted delivered him to the land of Filastin (Palestine). When it was the forenoon of the fourth day, they embalmed themselves (tahannatu, perfumed themselves with spices for burial) and shrouded themselves in anṭā' (leather hides), and then the Cry came upon them and they perished. It is also read as "al-ṣa'qah" (الصَّعْقَةُ), which is the single instance of the verb "ṣa'q" (striking down).

﴿while they were looking on﴾, at it, witnessing it directly.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 45:

﴿So they were not able to stand up [against it]﴾, like His saying, exalted is He: "﴿So they were found lying prostrate in their homes﴾" [Qur'an 7:78, cf. 11:67].

﴿And they were not ones who could be helped﴾ by others, just as they did not defend themselves by their own means.

And the people of Noah before them, [We destroyed]. That is: We destroyed the people of Noah, for what precedes it indicates it, or [it means] "remember." It is also permissible that it be in the accusative as a conjunction with the place of ʿAd, and the reading with the genitive (jarr) supports this. It has also been said that it is conjoined with the object of "fa-akhadhnāhu" (so We seized him).

﴿from before﴾: that is, from before these who were destroyed.

﴿Indeed they were a people of defiant transgression﴾: going beyond the bounds in what they were engaged in of disbelief and sins.

﴿And the heaven We built with might﴾, i.e., with strength.

﴿And indeed, We are expanding it﴾ (p-143) — capable. It is from *al-wus'* (السعة), in the sense of capacity or ability. *Al-Muwsi'* is one who is capable of spending. Or it means: We are expanding the heaven, or what lies between it and the earth, or the provision.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 48:

﴿And the earth — We have spread it out﴾ — We made it smooth and extended it so that they could settle upon it.

﴿How excellent are the ones who spread it﴾ — i.e., We.

And of everything We created pairs, so that you may take heed.

"And of everything" — i.e., of the kinds (of created things).

"Pairs" — i.e., two types, male and female, corresponding to one another: the heaven and the earth, the night and the day, the sun and the moon, the land and the sea, and the like.

"So that you may take heed" — i.e., We did all of that so that you would remember and recognize that He is the Creator of all and its Provider, that He alone deserves worship, and that He is able to bring all of them back, and so that you would act in accordance with that.

Its clause "So flee to Allah" (﴿فَفِرُّوا إلى اللَّهِ﴾) is governed by an implied saying, addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ) by way of *talwin* (a shift in mode of address). The "fa" (فاء) here is either for the sequencing of the command after what has been mentioned of the effects of His anger, which necessitate fleeing from them, and of the judgments of His mercy, which call for fleeing toward them. It is as if it were said: "Say to them: since the matter is so, then flee to Allah, whose affairs are these, through faith and obedience, so that you may be saved from His punishment and win His reward." Or the "fa" is for conjunction with an implied clause that follows His saying ﴿so that you may remember﴾ (﴿لَعَلَّكم تَذَكَّرُونَ﴾). It is as if it were said: "Say to them, 'Then remember,' so flee to Allah..." and so on.

His saying ﴿Indeed I am to you from Him a clear warner﴾ (﴿إنِّي لَكم مِنهُ نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ﴾) is a reason given for the command to flee to Him, or for the obligation to comply with it. His being (upon him be blessings and peace) a warner from Him, may He be exalted, necessitates that he command them to flee to Him, and that they comply. That is: "Indeed I am to you, on His behalf, a warner," between being a warner and being one who makes manifest what must be made manifest of the punishment with which he warns. In His command to the Messenger (ﷺ) to tell them to flee to Him from His punishment, and in His giving as the reason that he (upon him be blessings and peace) warns them on His behalf and not of his own accord, there is a gracious promise of their deliverance from what they flee and their success in what they seek.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 51:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not make with Allah another god﴾ is a prohibition that necessitates fleeing from the cause of punishment, after the command to flee from Him Himself, as His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, I am to you from Him﴾ suggests; that is, from the making (of a partner, al-ja'l) which is forbidden.

﴿a clear warner﴾. The connection of the word "min" (from) with "warning" (al-indhar), while its complement is normally "ba'" (with/of), is because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of "fleeing" (al-ifrar). It is said: "farra minhu" (he fled from him), meaning he ran away, and "afarrahu ghayruhu" (another made him flee). It is as if it were said: "And flee from making with Him, Exalted is He, any other god, either in belief or in speech." In this there is an emphasis on what precedes it, namely the command to flee from the punishment to Him, Exalted is He, but not by way of repetition as has been said; rather, by way of prohibiting its cause and making fleeing obligatory.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 52:

﴿Thus﴾ i.e., the matter is like what He mentioned of their denying the Messenger and calling him a sorcerer or a madman. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Not came to those before them﴾ ...etc. is an explanation of it, i.e., what came to them.

﴿any messenger﴾ from among the messengers of Allah.

﴿but they said﴾ about him,

﴿"A sorcerer or a madman!"﴾ There is no way to make the kaf (ka, "like") govern "atā" (came), because the word after the negating "mā" cannot act on what comes before it. (p-144)

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 53:

﴿Did they bequeath this to one another?﴾ This is a denunciation and an expression of wonder at their state and their unanimity upon that abominable saying, which hardly occurs to the mind of any sensible person, let alone is uttered by them. That is: some of them enjoined this saying upon others until they agreed upon it. And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Nay, but they are a people transgressing﴾ is a turning away (idrab, a shift of direction) from the matter of their agreement upon evil being based on their mutual enjoining of it, and an affirmation that it is a matter more heinous than mutual enjoining and more grievous than it: the transgression (tughyan) that encompasses all of them. This indicates that the utterance of that abominable saying from each one of them is in accordance with his wicked disposition (jibilla), not by the compulsion of a bequest from those before them, without that being the requirement of their natures.

**﴿So turn away from them﴾**: i.e., disregard their disputing with you, for you have repeatedly conveyed the call to them, and they have refused everything but refusal.

**﴿for you are not to be blamed﴾**: for turning away after you have exerted your utmost effort and gone beyond every customary limit in conveying the message.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 55:

﴿And remind, for indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾. That is: carry out the reminding and the admonition, and do not abandon them entirely; or, "so remind them." The object pronoun has been omitted because the matter is evident.

﴿For indeed the reminder benefits the believers﴾. That is: those whose faith Allah Most High has decreed, or those who have actually believed; for it increases them in insight (basirah) and strength in certainty (yaqin).

﴿And I did not create the jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me.﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (*istinaf*, an independent clause that follows on from what precedes it) that emphasizes the command and establishes the content of its causal explanation (*ta'lil*, the stated reason). That their creation is directed toward the worship of God, exalted is He, is something that prompts the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, to remind them, and it obliges them to take heed and be admonished. The mention of the creation of the jinn first is probably because they preceded humankind in existence. The meaning of their being created for His worship, exalted is He, is that He created them ready for it and fully able to perform it to the utmost degree of readiness and the most complete capacity, while worship is required of them, by treating the attainment of an end as it stands in relation to that of which it is the fruit as equivalent to the relation of a purpose to that of which it is the aim. For that God's acts lead to noble ends is beyond dispute. How could it not be so, since it is a mercy from Him, exalted is He, and a bounty upon His servants? What does not befit His exalted and majestic presence is to explain these acts by a purpose in the sense of a motive for the act, such that were it not for it He would not have done it, because that would lead to His perfection through the act, whereas He is perfect in act in every respect. But as for purpose in the sense of a perfective end to which the act of the true agent leads, this is not denied of His acts, exalted is He; rather all of them proceed in the right way. On this understanding His attribute of wisdom turns, and this measure suffices for the realization of the meaning of causation, as the jurists say and as the people of the language understand it, and by it the signification of the particle *lam* (of purpose) is realized. As for the agent's intention toward it, this is not among the requirements of the *lam*, such that the non-occurrence of worship from some would entail the non-fulfilment of what was intended by the intention. If some are hindered from reaching the end, despite the convergence of the principles and the interlocking of the premises that lead to it, this does not prevent it from being an end, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿A Book which We have sent down to you that you may bring mankind out of darknesses into the light﴾ and its like. It has also been said that the meaning is: "except that they might be commanded to worship Me," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they were not commanded except that they worship one God﴾. It has also been said that what is meant is: the happy ones of both kinds, just as what is meant by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly created for Hell many of the jinn and humankind﴾ is their wretched ones. What supports this is the reading of one who recited "And I did not create the jinn and humankind except from among the believers." Mujahid said, and al-Baghawi chose it: its meaning is "except that they might know Him." Its basis is the saying of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, in what he relates from the Lord of Might: "I was a hidden treasure, so I loved to be known, so I created the creation that I might be known." Perhaps the secret in expressing knowledge by worship, through the figure of speech that uses the name of the cause for the effect, is to alert to the fact that what is regarded is the knowledge gained through His worship, exalted is He, not what is attained by other means, such as the knowledge of the philosophers.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 57:

﴿I do not desire any provision from them, nor do I desire that they feed Me.﴾ This is an explanation that His (exalted is He) manner with His servants is far too exalted to be like the manner of masters with their slaves, who possess them so that they may be helped by them in obtaining their livelihoods and preparing their sustenance. That is to say: I do not desire to employ them in obtaining My provision or their own provision. Rather, I bestow upon them their provision and whatever sets them right and sustains them from My own side. So let them occupy themselves with that for which they were created, namely My worship.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 58:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the Provider﴾, who provides for everything that is in need of provision. It also contains an allusion that He is free of need of it. It is also read as "Indeed I am the Provider" (inni ana al-Razzaq).

﴿Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾. It is in the nominative (raf') on the basis that it is an adjective (na't) of al-Razzaq, or of "dhu" (possessor), or a predicate after a predicate (khabar ba'da khabar), or the predicate of an implied subject (khabar li-mudmar). It is also read in the genitive (jarr) on the basis that it is a description of "al-quwwah" (strength), under the interpretation of "al-iqtidar" (capability) or "al-ayd" (power).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 59:

﴿Indeed, for those who have done wrong﴾ That is: they have wronged themselves by exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment through denying the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); or they put denial in the place of affirmation. They are the people of Makkah.

﴿a portion﴾ That is: a full share of the punishment.

﴿like the portion of their companions﴾ Like the shares of their counterparts from the previous nations that were mentioned. It is derived from the image of water-carriers dividing the water by the dhanub (a great bucket, full), so the word is taken from that practice of sharing out water by buckets.

﴿So let them not ask Me to hasten it﴾ That is: let them not demand that I hasten its coming. It is said: "istaʿjalahu" meaning he urged him to hurry and commanded him to do so; and it is also said: "istaʿjalahu" meaning he sought its occurrence quickly. From it is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾. This is a reply to their saying: "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 51, verse 60:**

﴿So woe to those who disbelieve﴾. He placed the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in the place of their pronoun, to record upon them what is in the relative clause (silah) of disbelief, and to indicate the cause (`illah) of the ruling. The first fa' (the "so" in ﴿so woe﴾) indicates the sequential ordering (tartib) of the woe's establishment for them, on the basis that for them there is a great punishment, just as the first fa' indicates the ordering of the prohibition of seeking to hasten (the punishment) upon that. The "min" in His words, exalted is He, ﴿from their day which they are promised﴾, is for causation (ta'lil), meaning: they are promised it from the day of Badr. It has also been said: the Day of Resurrection, and this is more fitting with what is at the beginning of the forthcoming noble surah. The first (view) is more suitable to what precedes it, in that both of them are from the worldly punishment.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites al-Dhariyat, Allah, exalted is He, will give him ten good deeds for the number of every wind that blew and flowed in the world."
